passage: Yamini was picked to read out the group's poem in Hindi class, and I sat two seats from her, so I watched the whole thing. When Sir called her name, she went red from neck to forehead and looked at her paper as if it might rescue her. She spoke so softly the back row shouted "Louder!" Her voice shook, but she didn't stop. Then she gave a tiny laugh and read the last two lines with her hand covering half her face. At the break she told me she had rehearsed it in front of the mirror all week. I can't tell if she hated every second or secretly liked it. - Ramesh

qa.q: What did the back row shout at Yamini?
qa.a: The back row shouted 'Louder!'

qa.q: What might Yamini be feeling as she reads, and what else might be true?
qa.a: She is likely embarrassed and self-conscious, shown by her blushing and covering her face; she may also feel proud, since she kept going and had rehearsed all week.

qa.q: What small step could help Yamini feel more comfortable next time?
qa.a: She could read to one or two friends first, then to a small group, building comfort in tiny steps.

qa.q: How might the back row's shout have felt to Yamini?
qa.a: It may have added to her worry about how she seemed, or it may have felt like ordinary classroom noise; she could not easily tell which.

grounding: A shy teen blushes, avoids the spotlight and overthinks how she seems; small steps build comfort.

passage:
Day 1. Ayesha stood at the door of the drama club room, then walked past it. Her friend Keerthana had asked her to try a session, but Ayesha imagined everyone staring at her and left for the library.
Day 5. Keerthana said, "Just sit at the back with me. You don't have to do anything." Ayesha went, sat quietly, and her ears burned when the teacher glanced at her, but nobody paid attention.
Day 12. During a warm-up circle, Ayesha said her name and one favourite food, in a tiny voice. People clapped once and moved on. She walked home feeling lighter than she had in weeks.

qa.q: Where did Ayesha go instead of the drama club on day one?
qa.a: She went to the library.

qa.q: Why did Ayesha walk past the drama club room on day one?
qa.a: She imagined everyone staring at her, which reflects the self-consciousness that keeps her from going in.

qa.q: How did Keerthana make it easier for Ayesha to join in?
qa.a: Keerthana offered a small step, sitting at the back together with no pressure to do anything, so comfort could grow gradually.

qa.q: How might the other club members have seen Ayesha's tiny voice?
qa.a: They probably saw it as an ordinary introduction and clapped once before moving on, so it felt much bigger to her than to them.

grounding: A shy teen avoids the spotlight and builds comfort through small steps into a social situation.

passage:
Farida, you think your Wasim Nana was always this talkative? When I was fifteen, I couldn't even ask the shopkeeper for a pencil without my face going red.
In class I knew the answers, but I'd pretend I didn't. If the teacher called my name, my voice disappeared. I spent whole evenings replaying every word I'd said and thinking everyone had laughed.
My uncle noticed. He didn't force me onto a stage. He said, "One thing a day. Small."
Day one, I said "salaam" first to the milkman. Day two, I asked the price of mangoes. Week two, I read one line of poetry at a family dinner. My ears were burning, but I did it.
By the end of that year, I was reading the whole poem at the school function. Still nervous. But I could do it.
So, Farida, no stages yet. Just one small thing tomorrow.

qa.q: What did Wasim say first to the milkman?
qa.a: He said "salaam" first to the milkman.

qa.q: How did Wasim feel about speaking at fifteen?
qa.a: He felt painfully shy and self-conscious, his face going red and his voice disappearing, and he replayed his words all evening.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Wasim Nana's story?
qa.a: His uncle suggesting one small step a day, which slowly built comfort until he could read a whole poem at the school function.

qa.q: How might Wasim's uncle have seen his shyness?
qa.a: He seemed to understand it gently, choosing small steps instead of pushing Wasim onto a stage.

grounding: The elder's story shows a teenager's shyness and self-consciousness easing through small steps into social situations.

passage:
At his cousin's wedding in Indore, Samir had spent two hours standing against the wall, cheeks hot, sure everyone was looking at his too-big borrowed kurta.
Then the power went out in the middle of the sangeet. Screams, then laughter. Someone shouted for torches.
His aunt, Sangeeta Mami, found him in the dark. "Samir! Your phone has the best torch. Come, hold it for the dancers."
He froze. The dance floor. In front of everyone.
"You don't have to dance," she whispered. "Just stand at the edge and shine the light. That's all."
He took a breath and walked to the edge. His hand shook. But everyone was looking at the dancers, not him.
When the power came back, an uncle clapped him on the back. "Our lighting director!"
Samir laughed, surprised at himself. Later, when Mami pulled him in for the last song, he danced for half a minute before escaping, grinning.

qa.q: Where was the wedding?
qa.a: In Indore.

qa.q: What was Samir feeling as he stood against the wall?
qa.a: Samir felt shy and self-conscious, cheeks hot, sure everyone was judging his too-big kurta.

qa.q: Why did Sangeeta Mami's idea work?
qa.a: She gave him a small, useful job at the edge of the crowd, a manageable step that didn't put him in the spotlight.

qa.q: How might the guests have seen Samir holding the torch?
qa.a: Most were watching the dancers, and those who noticed, like the uncle, saw him as helpful, not awkward.

grounding: The scene shows a self-conscious teenager taking a small step into a social situation, which builds comfort.

passage:
Lalremsiami had come from Aizawl to a Delhi school in Class 9, and for the first month she barely spoke. When anyone looked at her, she blushed and looked at her notebook. At lunch she sat at the end of the bench and read.
Shalini, who sat in front of her, noticed. She didn't drag her into a crowd. On Monday she just turned around and said, "Can I borrow your ruler? Mine broke."
On Wednesday she asked, "What's the word for 'thank you' in Mizo?"
Lalremsiami told her, very quietly. Shalini tried it and got it wrong. Lalremsiami laughed, surprised at herself.
On Friday, in geography, the teacher asked about hills in the northeast. Lalremsiami's hand went halfway up, then down. Shalini whispered, "You'd know this best."
Lalremsiami raised her hand again. Her voice was soft, but she answered. And she didn't blush for long.

qa.q: Where had Lalremsiami come from?
qa.a: From Aizawl.

qa.q: What was Lalremsiami feeling in her first month?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt shy and self-conscious, blushing and looking at her notebook whenever anyone looked at her.

qa.q: What made Shalini's approach helpful?
qa.a: She took small, low-pressure steps, borrowing a ruler and asking a word, which built comfort before encouraging a bigger step in class.

qa.q: How might Shalini see her small steps with Lalremsiami?
qa.a: Shalini seems to see them as a gentle way to make friends without pushing someone shy into the spotlight.

grounding: The scene shows a shy teenager building comfort through small social steps.

passage:
"Everyone's looking at me," Jagdish muttered, tugging his kurta collar.
"Nobody's looking at you," Urmila-didi said. "They're looking at the paneer counter."
"My face is red. I can feel it."
"It's a wedding in May. Everyone's red. This shamiana is an oven."
"I'll just sit in the car."
"You sat in the car at the last three functions. Try one small thing. Just one. Then the car, if you want."
"Like what?"
"Say hi to Mani Mama. He's alone at the juice table. He loves trains. You don't even have to talk much. Just ask about a train."
Jagdish looked at the juice table as if it were a cliff edge. "And if I say something stupid?"
"Then he'll talk about trains anyway."
He took a breath and walked over. Four minutes later he was holding a sugarcane juice and nodding while Mani Mama drew a route map on a napkin. He glanced back and rolled his eyes, but he stayed.
"Car?" she mouthed.
He shook his head. "Later."

qa.q: Who was alone at the juice table?
qa.a: Mani Mama was alone at the juice table.

qa.q: What was Jagdish feeling as he tugged his collar?
qa.a: Jagdish felt self-conscious and embarrassed, sure everyone was looking at his red face; there was also worry about saying something stupid.

qa.q: Why was Urmila-didi's 'one small thing' a good suggestion?
qa.a: It gave Jagdish a tiny, safe step, one question about trains with a way out afterwards, which built comfort instead of pushing him into the crowd. 🙂

qa.q: How might Mani Mama have felt when Jagdish came over?
qa.a: Mani Mama, alone at the table, was probably pleased to have company, happily drawing a route map on a napkin.

grounding: It shows a teenager's blushing and self-consciousness at a family function, and a small step into conversation building comfort.
